question: SQ-LIP-000041
text: How does lipedema affect health-related quality of life?
minor_problems: [minor] set: P2's 'not clearly more than women with comparable obesity' is contradicted by E3 (BMI-matched controls) and E13, both listed as supporting under it; the clause should be separated or reworded.
[minor] set: E26 is not about liposuction yet is placed under P7; E6 and E17 are placed where they fit only partly (P2, P1) rather than P3 and P5.
[minor] set: P3 and P4 overlap in predictors (E7 covers depression, appearance distress, mobility and symptom severity); fatigue and pain prevalence (E21, E5) have no proposition.

[minor] P2: not fully supported; overgeneralized; two ideas; stance errors ['E3']; misplaced ['E6'] — suggested: Depressive and anxiety symptoms are frequently reported in people with lipedema, though evidence on whether they exceed those in women with comparable obesity is inconsistent. (Second clause ('not clearly more than comparable obesity') rests on one study (E10) and is contradicted by E3, where controls matched for BMI had far less depression (43.6 vs 18.5 percent; PHQ-8 89.7 vs 39.3 percent), yet E3 is labelled supporting the whole statement. E13 also cites behavioural disturbances versus overweight controls. Frequency and comparison clauses have different evidence. E6 is mostly about correlates of HRQoL (P3).)

[minor] P3: two ideas (Four correlates (depression, appearance distress, stigma, psychological flexibility) from cross-sectional regressions; association only and partly circular with the psychological WHOQOL domain. E6 (correlations with depression and appearance distress) supports this and is placed under P2.)

[minor] P5: stance errors ['E12', 'E18']; misplaced ['E17'] — suggested: Most studies report worse quality of life and psychological burden at more advanced stages, though one cohort found no stage differences. (Two stage-associated findings (E12, E18; E17 also reports worse physical and social functioning at higher stages) versus one null (E21): 'inconsistent' is defensible but understates the weight toward association. Stances 'supporting' for 'inconsistent' are confusing. Stage is self-reported in E12.)

[minor] P7: misplaced ['E26'] (E15 and E24 are uncontrolled pre-post series, so only association is claimed, which the wording respects. E26 (validation of a benefit index in lymphedema/lipedema) is not about liposuction and is misplaced.)

[minor] P8: not fully supported; overgeneralized — suggested: Disease-specific quality-of-life profiles of lipedema and lymphedema may differ, with inconsistent findings on mood and global quality of life. ('Lipedema worse on symptom, appearance and mood' rests on E25 alone; E9 found comparable depression and global QoL (but worse function in lymphedema) and is labelled contradicting, yet the wording does not reflect it.)

items.title: Mental and physical health burden and quality of life in Czech women with lipedema
items.quote: mais da metade apresenta sintomas depressivos moderados a severos e a qualidade de vida é baixa em múltiplos domínios, com o domínio psicológico o mais afetado
items.note: Cross-sectional observational study directly measuring depression (PHQ-9), quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF), and symptom associations in lipedema patients; small sample (n=43) and chi-square associations are unadjusted, limiting strength.
old_statements: In a cross-sectional study of 43 Czech women with lipedema, 50.9% had moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 >=10) and WHOQOL-BREF scores were low across domains (psychological 46.3, physical 50.8), with the psychological domain most affected; specific physical symptoms (shortness of breath, muscle stiffness, appetite problems, fatigue, numbness) were significantly associated with depression severity.

items.note: Online self-administered survey of lipedema patients reports quality of life, anxiety, and depression measures (HADS, SF-12), directly addressing the question, though stratified primarily by FMS comorbidity rather than lipedema vs controls.
old_statements: In a cross-sectional study of 354 women with lipedema, 35% met FMS criteria, and those with comorbid FMS had significantly higher anxiety (13.11 vs 9.87) and depression (10.23 vs 8.26) scores and lower SF-12 physical (35.37 vs 42.55) and mental (35.27 vs 40.38) quality-of-life scores (all p<0.001).

items.title: Health Implications of Lipedema: Analysis of Patient Questionnaires and Population-Based Matched Controls
items.quote: Depressao autorrelatada nos ultimos 12 meses em 43,6% do grupo lipedema vs 18,5% dos controles (p=0,001); pelo PHQ-8, apenas 10,3% dos pacientes nao tinham sintomas depressivos vs 60,7% dos controles
items.note: Cross-sectional questionnaire study with BMI/age/sex-matched controls directly measuring quality of life, depression (PHQ-8), pain and social outcomes in lipedema patients, showing significantly worse mental health and QoL outcomes. [grade capped moderate->low per curated Oxford N4]
old_statements: In a study comparing lipedema patients with population controls matched for sex, age and BMI, lipedema patients reported worse self-rated general health, higher rates of self-reported depression (43.6% vs 18.5%, p=0.001) with PHQ-8 depressive symptoms in 89.7% versus 39.3% of controls, more severe pain and pain-related disability, fewer close social contacts, and a strong positive correlation between pain severity and depressive symptoms (rho=0.612, p<0.001).

items.note: Cross-sectional online survey of women with lipedema directly measuring quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF) and depression (PHQ-9), with multivariate regression linking symptom burden to reduced QoL; directly addresses the question's affirmative  [grade capped moderate->low per curated Oxford N4]
old_statements: In a survey of 98 Polish women with lipedema, all WHOQOL-BREF domains scored below general-population values (physical health 45.4, psychological 46.3, social relationships 50.4, environment 49.6 on 0-100), 59.2% had PHQ-9 scores >=10 indicating possible depression (mean PHQ-9 12.2), and core lipedema symptoms (Factor 1: leg heaviness, joint/tissue/muscle pain, swelling, stiffness) were the only significant predictor of worse quality of life (beta=-0.345, p=0.004, model explaining 23.5% of variance).

items.title: Depression and appearance-related distress in functioning with lipedema
items.quote: Lower quality of life was predicted by higher symptom severity, lower mobility, higher appearance-related distress and higher depression severity. Appearance-related distress and depression constitute important aspects of psychological functioning in women with lipedema.
items.note: Cross-sectional online survey with validated psychometric instruments and hierarchical regression directly quantifies how depression, appearance distress and physical factors predict quality of life in lipedema patients, with adjusted (mult [grade capped moderate->low per curated Oxford N4]
old_statements: In 329 women with lipedema, lower quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF) was independently predicted by higher depression (PHQ-9 β=-0.36), higher appearance-related distress (DAS-24 β=-0.29), lower mobility (β=0.27) and higher symptom severity, with the final regression model explaining 73% of QoL variance and mean PHQ-9 of 11.87 indicating minor depression.

items.title: Health-related stigma, perceived social support, and their role in quality of life among women with lipedema
items.quote: we found significantly more health-related stigma compared to an aged-matched general female population (N = 1872), leading to an overall lower quality of life. Conversely, strong social support was associated with better social and emotional functioning.
items.note: The article directly examines quality of life and emotional well-being in lipedema patients, reporting that higher stigma is associated with lower HRQoL and worse emotional functioning, supporting the question's affirmative direction regard [grade capped moderate->low per curated Oxford N4]
old_statements: In a cross-sectional survey of 245 women with lipedema, health-related stigma was significantly higher than in an age-matched general female population (Distress 49.5 vs 17.1–28.7; 65% with moderate/severe distress) and correlated negatively with all RAND-36 quality-of-life domains (strongest for social functioning r=−0.54 and emotional well-being r=−0.50), while greater perceived social support correlated positively with HRQoL.

items.title: Stages of lipoedema: experiences of physical and mental health and health care

old_statements: In a survey of lipedema patients comparing self-reported stages, more advanced stage (3-4) was associated with higher rates of depression (48.3% vs 34.8%, p<0.001), social isolation (staying home 64.3% vs 44.4%), life dissatisfaction (35.7% vs 22.0%), and loss of mobility, while psychological burden such as inferiority complex (72.8%) and constantly thinking about lipedema (73.4%) was high across all stages.

items.title: Lipedema: The intersection of physical and mental health
items.quote: pacientes com lipedema mostraram dificuldade significativamente maior na regulação emocional e níveis mais altos de ansiedade
items.note: Narrative review (no original intervention) summarizing observational and survey studies that consistently report impaired quality of life, elevated anxiety, depressive symptoms, and emotional/behavioral disturbances in lipedema patients, d
old_statements: This narrative review synthesizing 25 references reports that lipedema patients show greater emotional dysregulation and higher anxiety (Al-Wardat: 26 patients vs 26 controls via DERS/HAM-A), significant behavioral disturbances versus overweight/obese controls (Chachaj et al.), depressive/anxious symptoms associated with comorbid fibromialgia (Cagliyan Turk et al.), occupational limitations in 51–73% of respondents (Clarke et al.), and that liposuction significantly reduced depressive symptoms and improved quality of life and body image (Arndt et al.).

items.title: Health-related quality of life among lipedema patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.quote: Emotional well-being: 64,19 (IC 95% 59,86–68,52) vs norma 73,2 — ansiedade/depressão frequentes; I²=89,41%

old_statements: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of cross-sectional cohorts, women with lipedema showed reduced HRQoL across all SF-36/RAND-36 domains versus population norms, with the largest deficits in energy/fatigue (43.50 vs 59.4), bodily pain (51.77 vs 77.4), role physical (51.10 vs 82.4), and general health (49.64 vs 73.1), plus impaired emotional well-being (64.19 vs 73.2) reflecting frequent anxiety/depression.

items.title: Quality of life following liposuction for lipoedema: a prospective outcome study

old_statements: In a prospective study of lipedema patients undergoing power-assisted liposuction, PHQ-4 total scores fell from 4.47 (mild depression, above population norm) to 2.10 (p<0.001), with anxiety subscale dropping 2.47→0.93 and depression subscale 2.00→1.17, while quality-of-life satisfaction (FLZM health module 45.77→88.00), self-esteem (RSES 29.93→33.33), and emotional stability all improved significantly postoperatively.

items.title: Women with lipoedema: a national survey on their health, health-related quality of life, and sense of coherence
items.quote: Mulheres com lipedema pontuaram 25–35 pontos ABAIXO da população feminina sueca geral em TODAS as subescalas do RAND-36, em todos os grupos etários (p<0,05 na maioria). A menor diferença foi em bem-estar emocional (~10 pontos)

items.note: Large cross-sectional study using validated PROMs (WHOQOL-BREF, PHQ-9) directly quantifying quality of life and depression in lipedema patients, with stage-dependent correlations; directly addresses the question's affirmative direction.
old_statements: In 511 lipedema patients, PHQ-9 averaged 10.84±6.39 with 54% at risk of moderate-to-severe depression, WHOQOL-BREF global score averaged 60.5±16.02 (lowest in physical 54.54 and psychological 51.91 domains), and quality-of-life impairment correlated with disease stage (r=0.55, p<0.001) and inversely with depression score (r=-0.775, p<0.0001).

old_statements: In 511 lipedema patients, PHQ-9 averaged 10.84±6.39 with 54% at risk of moderate-to-severe depression, WHOQOL-BREF global score averaged 60.5±16.02 (lowest in physical 54.54 and psychological 51.91 domains), and quality-of-life impairment correlated with disease stage (r=0.55, p<0.001) and inversely with depression score (r=-0.775, p<0.0001).

items.title: Clinical characteristics, comorbidities, and correlation with advanced lipedema stages: A retrospective study from a Swiss referral centre
items.quote: Burden psicossocial elevado (n=239): ansiedade (HADS≥8) 64,4%; depressão (HADS≥8) 23,4%; fadiga alta (FSS≥4) 56,1%; dor alta (BPI≥7) 14,2%; QV baixa: PCS-SF36 em 71,5%, MCS-SF36 em 67,4% — NENHUM desses parâmetros diferiu significativamente entre estágios (p>0,5)
items.note: Retrospective referral-centre study with validated instruments (SF-36, HADS, BPI, FSS) directly quantifying quality of life, depression, and anxiety in lipedema patients, showing high psychosocial burden dissociated from disease stage.
old_statements: In a Swiss cohort of 239 lipedema patients assessed with validated questionnaires, 64.4% had anxiety (HADS≥8), 23.4% had depression (HADS≥8), and low quality of life was found in 71.5% (PCS-SF36) and 67.4% (MCS-SF36), with none of these psychosocial parameters differing significantly across disease stages (p>0.5).

items.title: Lipedema in Sweden – “The LISE-study”: Quality of life and body image in women with lipedema compared to healthy controls and women with cancer
items.quote: Women with lipedema experienced significantly more symptoms than healthy controls, including more pain, fatigue, depression, anxiety, loss of appetite, dyspnea and reduced QoL (<0.001 for all).
items.note: Study directly measures quality of life, body image, depression and anxiety in lipedema patients versus controls, finding significantly worse outcomes across all measures.
old_statements: In a comparative cross-sectional study, women with lipedema (n=104) had significantly lower HR-QoL (RAND-36) than healthy controls across all eight dimensions (p<0.001), scores comparable to women with advanced cancer in several dimensions (even lower in general health), greater body image concern (BSQ, p=0.001), and higher symptom burden including depression and anxiety (ESAS, p<0.001).

items.title: A qualitative study exploring the experiences of individuals living with lipoedema and the impacts it has on their quality of life.
items.quote: Individuals living with lipoedema experience impacts on their quality-of-life across physical, psychological, and social aspects of life.
items.note: Qualitative study directly exploring how lipoedema affects quality of life across physical, psychological, and social domains, supporting the affirmative direction; psychological burden addressed though not via standardized depression/anxie
old_statements: In a qualitative study of 16 individuals with lipoedema, participants reported impacts on quality of life across physical, psychological, and social domains, driven by symptom burden, social judgement, and healthcare-related challenges.

items.title: Improvement in Health-Related Quality of Life and Symptoms Following Lipedema Liposuction: A Longitudinal Study
items.quote: liposuction is an effective treatment for improving HRQoL and symptoms in lipedema patients, although it may not completely restore HRQoL to normative levels
items.note: The study reports symptomatic and quality-of-life improvement after liposuction, supporting a modification of disease burden, but explicitly notes it may not fully restore HRQoL to normal levels — a qualified/narrower claim, not a cure, hen
old_statements: In 76 UK women with lipedema (mean follow-up 25.3 months), liposuction produced significant postoperative improvement across all SF-36 and WHOQOL-BREF domains and all 17 Lipedema Symptom Scale items (P<0.001), but SF-36 physical, social, and general health scores remained below age-matched normative levels.

items.title: A retrospective cross-sectional study comparing health-related quality-of-life in females with lipoedema and bilateral leg lymphoedema.
items.quote: LSIDS-L — Lipedema scored worse in: sensação neurológica (2,67 ± 2,22 vs 1,88 ± 2,22; p=0,003; rB=0,29) refletindo dor alodínica/neuropática, picadas e formigamento
items.note: The study found lipoedema and lymphoedema differ in specific HRQoL outcomes while sharing similar symptoms, supporting a qualified distinction between the conditions but only via patient-reported outcomes, not pathophysiology.
old_statements: In 151 women, those with lipoedema (N=90) reported significantly higher LYMQOL-leg burden scores for symptoms (p=0.003), appearance (p=0.003) and mood (p=0.011), and worse LSIDS-L neurological, biobehavioral and resource scores than those with bilateral leg lymphoedema (N=61), indicating distinguishable HRQoL profiles despite similar symptoms.

items.title: Evaluation of Patient-relevant Outcomes of Lymphedema and Lipedema Treatment: Development and Validation of a New Benefit Tool
items.quote: Global and subscale scores correlated with convergent criteria and with change in disease-specific HRQoL, but not with change in generic HRQoL.
items.note: The article develops and validates a measurement instrument involving lymphedema and lipedema combined; it measures treatment benefit and correlates with HRQoL but does not itself test how lipedema specifically affects HRQoL versus controls
old_statements: A new disease-specific Patient Benefit Index for lymphedema and lipedema (PBI-L) was validated (n=301 cross-sectional, n=82 RCT), yielding a mean global benefit score of 2.2±1.0 and correlating with disease-specific HRQoL (FLQA-LK, r=0.31) but not with change in generic EQ-5D-3L.

items.title: Lipedema: pathophysiological insights and therapeutic strategies — An update for dermatologists
items.quote: The condition often coexists with psychological distress, which significantly detracts from the quality of life of affected individuals.
items.note: The review mentions anxiety/depression comorbidity and pain, which relate to quality of life, but it is a narrative synthesis that does not itself measure HRQoL, so it provides on-topic background rather than a direct test of the relationsh
old_statements: This review states that lipedema often coexists with psychological distress, which significantly detracts from the quality of life of affected individuals, and that psychological support is vital in addressing the emotional challenges of the condition.

propositions.statement: Health-related quality of life in lipedema is reduced across physical, psychological and social domains compared with population norms or healthy controls.
propositions.rationale: A meta-analysis and several cross-sectional studies show lower generic scores than norms or controls; heterogeneity is high and most norm comparisons are not BMI-matched.

evidence.finding: Meta-analysis of cross-sectional cohorts: reduced SF-36/RAND-36 scores in all domains vs norms; largest deficits in energy/fatigue (43.50 vs 59.4), bodily pain (51.77 vs 77.4), role physical (51.10 vs 82.4); I2=89%.

National Swedish survey: RAND-36 scores 25-35 points below age-matched general female population in all subscales; smallest gap in emotional well-being; worse physical and social functioning at higher stages.
RAND-36 total 59.3 vs 74.9 in Dutch women (p<0.001) and EQ-5D-3L 66.1 vs 85; anxiety/depression in 42.0% and pain/discomfort in 74.1%.
Women with lipedema (n=104) had lower RAND-36 scores than healthy controls in all eight dimensions (p<0.001), comparable to advanced cancer in several, plus greater body image concern.
In 44 women, median SF-36 total 57.4/100 (general health 35, energy 45, pain 47.5), below a healthy population reference; scores did not differ by BMI or WHtR strata.
Scoping review cites EQ-5D-3L 66.1 vs 85 and RAND-36 59.3 vs 74.9 vs Dutch population, difficulty in daily activities in 64.8%.
Qualitative interviews with 16 individuals: impacts on physical, psychological and social quality of life driven by symptoms, social judgement and healthcare challenges.
Review states lipedema often coexists with psychological distress that significantly detracts from quality of life.

propositions.statement: Depressive and anxiety symptoms are frequently reported in people with lipedema, though evidence on whether they exceed those in women with comparable obesity is inconsistent.
propositions.rationale: Validated screening tools report high frequencies versus population controls, with wide variation; the one comparison against overweight or obese women found no excess.

evidence.finding: Vs population controls matched for sex, age and BMI: self-reported depression 43.6% vs 18.5% (p=0.001); PHQ-8 depressive symptoms in 89.7% vs 39.3%.
In 43 Czech women, 50.9% had moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 >=10); WHOQOL-BREF psychological domain most affected (46.3).
Narrative review reports greater emotional dysregulation and higher anxiety than controls, behavioural disturbances vs overweight controls, and occupational limitations.
Narrative review: anxiety/depression in 42.0%; HRQoL inversely correlated with symptom severity (r=-0.651), depression (r=-0.750) and appearance distress (r=-0.654) in the largest cohort.

Vs overweight/obese women, no significant differences in depression or anxiety (BDI-II 11 vs 8, p=0.130; HADS-A p=0.162) before or after BMI adjustment, while WHO-DAS II disability was greater (social participation p=0.002).

propositions.statement_before_arbitration: Depressive and anxiety symptoms are frequently reported in people with lipedema, though not clearly more than in women with comparable obesity.

propositions.statement: Lower quality of life in lipedema is associated with psychological factors such as depression, appearance-related distress, stigma and low psychological flexibility.
propositions.rationale: Cross-sectional regression and correlation analyses; associational, with possible reverse causation and overlap between depression and quality-of-life measures.

evidence.finding: In 329 women, lower WHOQOL-BREF independently predicted by depression (beta=-0.36), appearance distress (beta=-0.29), lower mobility and symptom severity; model explained 73% of variance.
In 112 women, symptom severity explained 13.9% of QoL variance; psychological flexibility (beta=0.26) and social connectedness (beta=0.37) raised explained variance to 44.4%.

In 245 women, health-related stigma was higher than in age-matched general women and correlated negatively with all RAND-36 domains (social functioning r=-0.54); social support associated with better functioning.

propositions.statement: Pain and core physical symptom severity are associated with lower quality of life in lipedema.
propositions.rationale: Separate cross-sectional analyses identify pain and core symptoms as predictors; one source is a preprint.

evidence.finding: In a lipedema cohort, pain was the dominant driver negatively affecting physical, mental, environmental and general health, while physical activity positively affected mental and general health.

In 98 Polish women, all WHOQOL-BREF domains below general-population values; core symptoms (heaviness, pain, swelling, stiffness) were the only significant predictor of worse QoL (beta=-0.345, p=0.004).

propositions.statement: Findings are inconsistent on whether quality-of-life and psychological burden worsen with more advanced lipedema stage.
propositions.rationale: Self-reported stage comparisons and one stage correlation point to worse outcomes at advanced stages, while a moderate-grade cohort with validated tools found no stage differences.

evidence.finding: Stage 3-4 vs 1-2: depression 48.3% vs 34.8% (p<0.001), staying home 64.3% vs 44.4%, life dissatisfaction 35.7% vs 22.0%; inferiority feelings high across stages.
In 511 patients, QoL impairment correlated with stage (r=0.55, p<0.001) and PHQ-9 with stage (r=0.2, p=0.002); PHQ-9 mean 10.84, 54% at risk of moderate-to-severe depression.
In 239 patients, anxiety 64.4%, depression 23.4%, low PCS-SF36 71.5% and MCS-SF36 67.4%, with none of these differing significantly across disease stages (p>0.5).

propositions.statement: Comorbid fibromyalgia may be associated with further reduced quality of life and more anxiety and depression in lipedema.
propositions.rationale: One large cross-sectional study shows worse mental and physical scores in the fibromyalgia subgroup, a distinct modifier of quality of life.

evidence.finding: In 354 women, those with fibromyalgia (35%) had higher anxiety (13.11 vs 9.87) and depression (10.23 vs 8.26) and lower SF-12 physical (35.37 vs 42.55) and mental (35.27 vs 40.38) scores (p<0.001).

propositions.statement: Liposuction for lipedema is associated with improved health-related quality of life and psychological symptoms, although not always to normative levels.
propositions.rationale: Prospective and cohort data show postoperative improvement in quality of life and distress, with residual deficits versus norms.

evidence.finding: After power-assisted liposuction, PHQ-4 fell from 4.47 to 2.10 (p<0.001), indistinguishable from norm; FLZM health satisfaction 45.77 to 88.00; self-esteem improved.
In 76 UK women (mean follow-up 25.3 months), all SF-36 and WHOQOL-BREF domains improved (P<0.001), but physical, social and general health remained below age-matched norms.
A disease-specific Patient Benefit Index for lymphedema and lipedema was validated (n=301; n=82 RCT), correlating with disease-specific but not generic HRQoL change.

propositions.statement: Lipedema and lymphedema may differ in disease-specific quality-of-life profile, with lipedema reported worse on symptom, appearance and mood domains.
propositions.rationale: One retrospective comparison supports a distinct profile; another found overall quality of life and depression comparable, with worse function in lymphedema.

evidence.finding: In 151 women, lipoedema (n=90) had higher LYMQOL-leg burden for symptoms (p=0.003), appearance (p=0.003) and mood (p=0.011) and worse LSIDS-L neurological scores than bilateral lymphoedema (n=61).
37 lipedema vs 36 lymphedema women: depression (PHQ-9 10.4) and global QoL (LYMQOL-Leg) comparable; lymphedema had worse function (LEFS) and life satisfaction.

verdicts.note: Meta-analysis plus several national surveys and controlled comparisons agree; heterogeneity (I2 about 89 percent) noted in the finding; E5 correctly secondary of E20.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Depressive and anxiety symptoms are frequently reported in people with lipedema, though evidence on whether they exceed those in women with comparable obesity is inconsistent.
verdicts.note: Second clause ('not clearly more than comparable obesity') rests on one study (E10) and is contradicted by E3, where controls matched for BMI had far less depression (43.6 vs 18.5 percent; PHQ-8 89.7 vs 39.3 percent), yet E3 is labelled supporting the whole statement. E13 also cites behavioural disturbances versus overweight controls. Frequency and comparison clauses have different evidence. E6 is mostly about correlates of HRQoL (P3).

Four correlates (depression, appearance distress, stigma, psychological flexibility) from cross-sectional regressions; association only and partly circular with the psychological WHOQOL domain. E6 (correlations with depression and appearance distress) supports this and is placed under P2.
E19 and E4 support; E7 (symptom severity, mobility) and E16 (symptom severity explains part of QoL variance) also fit. Association only.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Most studies report worse quality of life and psychological burden at more advanced stages, though one cohort found no stage differences.
verdicts.note: Two stage-associated findings (E12, E18; E17 also reports worse physical and social functioning at higher stages) versus one null (E21): 'inconsistent' is defensible but understates the weight toward association. Stances 'supporting' for 'inconsistent' are confusing. Stage is self-reported in E12.
Single cross-sectional study (E2) with comparison inside lipedema; hedged 'may be associated'.

E15 and E24 are uncontrolled pre-post series, so only association is claimed, which the wording respects. E26 (validation of a benefit index in lymphedema/lipedema) is not about liposuction and is misplaced.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Disease-specific quality-of-life profiles of lipedema and lymphedema may differ, with inconsistent findings on mood and global quality of life.
verdicts.note: 'Lipedema worse on symptom, appearance and mood' rests on E25 alone; E9 found comparable depression and global QoL (but worse function in lymphedema) and is labelled contradicting, yet the wording does not reflect it.

set_issues.issue: P2's 'not clearly more than women with comparable obesity' is contradicted by E3 (BMI-matched controls) and E13, both listed as supporting under it; the clause should be separated or reworded.
E26 is not about liposuction yet is placed under P7; E6 and E17 are placed where they fit only partly (P2, P1) rather than P3 and P5.
P3 and P4 overlap in predictors (E7 covers depression, appearance distress, mobility and symptom severity); fatigue and pain prevalence (E21, E5) have no proposition.
